title: Chapter 72 — The Monkey-Rope
paragraphs: In the tumultuous business of cutting-in and attending to a whale, there is much running back and forth among the crew. Now hands are wanted here, and then again hands are wanted there. There is no staying in any one place; for at one and the same time everything has to be done everywhere. It is much the same with anyone who tries to describe the scene. We must now retrace our steps a little. It was mentioned that, on first breaking ground in the whale's back, the blubber-hook was inserted into the original hole cut there by the spades of the mates. But how did so clumsy and weighty a mass as that hook get fixed in that hole? It was put there by my particular friend Queequeg, whose duty it was, as harpooner, to go down onto the monster's back for that special purpose. But in very many cases circumstances require the harpooner to remain on the whale until the whole flensing, or stripping, operation is finished. The whale, mind you, lies almost entirely submerged, except for the parts being worked on. So down there, some ten feet below the level of the deck, the poor harpooner flounders about, half on the whale and half in the water, as the vast mass revolves like a treadmill beneath him. On the occasion in question, Queequeg appeared in Highland costume — a shirt and socks — in which, to my eyes at least, he looked uncommonly well; and no one had a better chance to observe him, as will soon be seen.

As the savage's bowsman — that is, the man who pulled the bow-oar in his boat (the second from the front) — it was my cheerful job to look after him while he did his hard-scrabble scrambling on the dead whale's back. You have seen Italian organ-grinder boys holding a dancing ape on a long cord. In just the same way, from the ship's steep side, I held Queequeg down there in the sea by what the fishery technically calls a monkey-rope, fastened to a strong strip of canvas belted around his waist.

It was a comically dangerous business for both of us. For before we go any further, I should explain that the monkey-rope was fastened at both ends: to Queequeg's broad canvas belt and to my narrow leather one. So for better or worse, the two of us were, for the time being, married; and if poor Queequeg sank never to rise again, both custom and honor required that the cord not be cut, but that it drag me down after him. In short, we were joined by a stretched-out Siamese ligature. Queequeg was my own inseparable twin brother, and there was no way for me to escape the dangerous liabilities that the hempen bond carried with it.

So strongly and metaphysically did I conceive of my situation then that, while earnestly watching his motions, I seemed distinctly to perceive that my own individuality was now merged in a joint-stock company of two; that my free will had received a mortal wound; and that another's mistake or misfortune might plunge innocent me into undeserved disaster and death. Therefore, I saw that here was a sort of interregnum in Providence; for its even-handed fairness never could have allowed so gross an injustice. And yet, still further pondering — while I jerked him now and then from between the whale and the ship, which threatened to jam him — still further pondering, I say, I saw that this situation of mine was the precise situation of every mortal that breathes; only, in most cases, he, one way or another, has this Siamese connection with a plurality of other mortals. If your banker breaks, you snap; if your apothecary by mistake sends you poison in your pills, you die. True, you may say that by exceeding caution you may possibly escape these and the countless other evil chances of life. But however carefully I handled Queequeg's monkey-rope, sometimes he jerked it so that I came very near sliding overboard. Nor could I possibly forget that, whatever I did, I had the management of only one end of it.*

*Every whaler has a monkey-rope; but only on the Pequod were the monkey and his holder ever tied together. This improvement on the usual practice was introduced by no less a man than Stubb, to give the endangered harpooner the firmest possible guarantee that whoever held his monkey-rope would be faithful and alert.

I have hinted that I often had to jerk poor Queequeg out from between the whale and the ship, where he would sometimes fall because of the ceaseless rolling and swaying of both. But that was not the only crushing danger he faced. Not at all put off by the slaughter inflicted on them during the night, the rabid sharks, now drawn afresh and more keenly by the blood that had been pent up until then and was starting to flow from the carcass, swarmed around it like bees in a hive.

And right in among those sharks was Queequeg, often shoving them aside with his floundering feet. That would be quite unbelievable, except that when the shark, which will otherwise eat almost anything, is drawn by prey like a dead whale, it will seldom touch a man.

Still, you can well believe that since the sharks have such a greedy finger in the pie, it is considered only sensible to keep a close watch on them. So, besides the monkey-rope, with which I now and then jerked the poor fellow away when he got too close to the jaws of some especially ferocious-looking shark, he had yet another protection. Hanging over the side in one of the stages, Tashtego and Daggoo kept waving a pair of sharp whale-spades over his head and killed as many sharks as they could reach. This was, to be sure, very unselfish and kind of them. They wanted Queequeg's greatest happiness, I admit; but in their hasty zeal to help him, and because he and the sharks were sometimes half hidden in the blood-clouded water, those careless spades of theirs came closer to cutting off a leg than a tail. But poor Queequeg, I suppose, straining and gasping there with that great iron hook — poor Queequeg, I suppose, just prayed to his Yojo and put his life in the hands of his gods.

Well, well, my dear comrade and twin brother, I thought, as I hauled in the rope and then let it out with every swell of the sea — what does it matter, after all? Aren't you the precious image of each and every one of us men in this whaling world? That unfathomed ocean you gasp in is Life; those sharks are your enemies; those spades, your friends; and between sharks and spades you are in a sorry pickle and peril, poor lad.

But courage! There is good cheer in store for you, Queequeg. For now, as with blue lips and bloodshot eyes the exhausted savage at last climbs up the chains and stands all dripping and involuntarily trembling over the side, the steward comes forward and, with a kindly, consoling glance, hands him — what? Some hot cognac? No! He hands him — ye gods! — he hands him a cup of lukewarm ginger and water!

"Ginger? Do I smell ginger?" Stubb asked suspiciously, coming near. "Yes, this must be ginger," peering into the as yet untasted cup. Then, standing as if in disbelief for a while, he calmly walked toward the astonished steward, slowly saying, "Ginger? ginger? And will you have the goodness to tell me, Mr. Dough-Boy, where the virtue of ginger lies? Ginger! Is ginger the sort of fuel you use, Dough-Boy, to kindle a fire in this shivering cannibal? Ginger! — what the devil is ginger? Sea-coal? Firewood? — lucifer matches? — tinder? — gunpowder? — what the devil is ginger, I say, that you offer this cup to our poor Queequeg here?"

"There is some sneaking Temperance Society movement behind this business," he suddenly added, now approaching Starbuck, who had just come from forward. "Will you look at that little can, sir? Smell it, if you please." Then, watching the mate's face, he added, "The steward, Mr. Starbuck, had the nerve to offer that calomel and jalap to Queequeg there, just this instant off the whale. Is the steward an apothecary, sir? And may I ask whether this is the sort of bitters with which he blows the life back into a half-drowned man?"
"I trust not," said Starbuck. "It is poor stuff enough."

"Aye, aye, steward," cried Stubb. "We'll teach you to drug a harpooner! None of your apothecary's medicine here! You want to poison us, do you? You've got life insurance on us and want to murder us all and pocket the money, do you?"
"It was not me," cried Dough-Boy. "It was Aunt Charity that brought the ginger on board, and told me never to give the harpooners any spirits, but only this ginger-jub — so she called it."

"Ginger-jub! You gingerly rascal! Take that! And run along with you to the lockers, and get something better. I hope I do no wrong, Mr. Starbuck. It is the captain's orders — grog for the harpooner on a whale."
"Enough," replied Starbuck. "Only don't hit him again, but —"
"Oh, I never hurt when I hit, except when I hit a whale or something of that sort. And this fellow's a weasel. What were you about to say, sir?"
"Only this: go down with him, and get what you want yourself."

Stubb came back with a dark flask in one hand and a kind of tea-caddy in the other. The flask held strong liquor and was passed to Queequeg; the caddy was Aunt Charity's present, and that was generously handed over to the waves.
